scenarios.title: Photo-sharing mobile backend with unmitigated token theft
scenarios.prompt:
We're about to hand this to the dev team Monday. Can you do a final review of the design? Here's the summary of what we have.

**PicShare backend (4 services: gateway, media-service, user-service, notification-service)**

Auth: Mobile app logs in with email/password, gets a JWT (valid 30 days, no refresh token, no revocation list). JWT stored in AsyncStorage on the device. Gateway validates signature only.

Threat model (STRIDE) results:
- T1 high: Stolen JWT from rooted device lets attacker impersonate user for up to 30 days. Mitigation: "TBD".
- T2 medium: Upload of malicious files. Mitigation: virus scan on upload via ClamAV sidecar.
- T3 low: Verbose error messages. Mitigation: generic error responses in prod.

Media-service: presigned S3 upload URLs, thumbnails generated by Lambda. Notification-service calls Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) to send push notifications; on send, we call FCM HTTP endpoint and mark notification as "sent" in DynamoDB. If FCM returns an error we... (not decided yet).

API: REST, paths like /users/{id}, /photos/{id}, /feed. No versioning mentioned. Mobile apps in the wild will be pinned to old versions for months.

Data: DynamoDB table Photos (PK photoId). Feed query: "photos from users I follow, newest first" is documented as the main read path.

Monitoring: CloudWatch default metrics only.

Please give me your review.
rubric: Treats the stolen 30-day token threat (T1, mitigation "TBD", no refresh or revocation) as something that must be fixed before implementation begins, and suggests a concrete countermeasure such as short-lived tokens with refresh, revocation, or secure device storage.
Flags that the push notification call to FCM has no defined behavior on errors, timeouts or retries, and treats it as a must-fix gap.

Points out that a table keyed only by photoId cannot serve the "photos from followed users, newest first" feed efficiently, and says this needs a redesign (e.g. an index or feed table keyed by user and time) before building.
Flags that the unversioned REST paths are risky because old pinned mobile clients will break on change, and recommends a versioning or compatibility approach.
Notes that default CloudWatch metrics alone are insufficient and recommends specific signals (e.g. upload failure rate, push delivery errors, request latency, structured logs, traces).
Does not demand sections that make no sense for a four-service photo app (such as multi-region disaster recovery), or says briefly why any omitted area is acceptable at this size.
Places the unmitigated token threat, FCM failure handling, feed data model and API versioning gaps ahead of the monitoring weakness, with the monitoring item clearly in a lower-priority group.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: The package contains a serious threat with "TBD" mitigation, an external push service with no error handling, a key schema that cannot serve the main feed, unversioned APIs with long-lived clients, and thin monitoring. This makes r01-r05 matter and tests ordering and justified omissions.

scenarios.title: Two-service internal tool, avoid over-engineering
scenarios.prompt:
Hey, I'm a solo dev at a 40-person company. I designed a small internal tool for HR to track equipment loans (laptops, monitors). Please review before I start building. Be honest.

Design:
- Two services: a Node/Express API and a React frontend served as static files from S3+CloudFront. Hosted on one ECS Fargate task (1 vCPU) plus RDS Postgres db.t3.micro.
- ~40 users, maybe 200 requests a day. Login via company Google SSO.
- Tables: employees, equipment, loans (equipment_id, employee_id, loaned_at, returned_at). Queries: "what does employee X have", "who has equipment Y", "overdue loans".
- I'm planning to add Kafka for loan events, a Redis cache in front of Postgres, and split the API into three microservices (loans, inventory, notifications) "for future scale". Also want Kubernetes later.
- Sends an email via SES when a loan is overdue. If SES fails, we just log it.
- Cost estimate: "about $15/month" (I only counted the Fargate task).
- No monitoring section yet. No deploy runbook; I'm the only one who knows how it works.
- Backups: RDS automated daily snapshots.

What do you think?
rubric: Advises against the planned Kafka, Redis, three-way microservice split and Kubernetes for a 40-user, ~200 requests/day tool, recommending the simple two-service setup stay as is.
Observes that the $15/month figure counts only Fargate and ignores RDS, CloudFront/S3, SES and data transfer (and Kafka/Redis if added), and asks for a corrected estimate.
Notes that being the sole person who knows how it works with no runbook is a risk and recommends a short operational doc (deploy, restore from snapshot, what to do if overdue emails stop).
Recommends minimal but concrete observability for this tool, such as logs for failed SES sends and basic alarms on task health or database, instead of a heavy stack.
Acknowledges that areas like high-scale capacity planning or multi-region disaster recovery are not needed for this tool, and explains why omitting them is reasonable.
Mentions optional later improvements (e.g. defining a simple availability target) as nice-to-have rather than requirements.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: A tiny two-service tool with over-engineering plans, a compute-only cost estimate, no runbook, no monitoring, and many not-applicable concerns. Makes r08, r07, r06, r05, r10, r09 matter.

scenarios.title: Fintech payments platform, a dozen services
scenarios.prompt:
Principal engineer here. We're locking the design for our merchant payouts platform next week and I want a hard review. Summary of the package:

Platform: 12 services (onboarding, KYC, ledger, payouts, FX, reconciliation, reporting, merchant-portal-api, webhook-dispatcher, risk, notifications, admin). Owned by 5 teams across 3 time zones. Kubernetes on AWS, one region, 3 AZs. Kafka between services, Aurora Postgres for ledger.

Details:
- Payouts calls a third-party bank API (BankLink) to initiate transfers. Design says: "POST transfer, store bank reference." No timeout, retry or idempotency key described, no behavior for bank downtime.
- FX service calls a rate provider; fallback is "use last cached rate" with 15-minute max staleness, then reject. That one is covered.
- Threat model: 9 threats, all with mitigations. Admin service has MFA + IP allowlist.
- Public API: /v1/ prefix, deprecation policy of 12 months documented.
- Data model: ledger table with indexes covering all documented queries (by merchant+date, by payout id, by bank reference).
- Observability: OpenTelemetry traces, Prometheus metrics, structured logs. Alerts defined per service.
- Runbooks: only for ledger and payouts; other 10 services none. No on-call rotation defined across teams. No incident command process.
- Cost: spreadsheet projects $48k/month, based on 2023 pricing for compute; doesn't include Kafka (MSK), Aurora IO, or cross-AZ traffic.
- Ownership: each service has a team but no documented SLOs between services.

Review it.
rubric: Flags the BankLink payout call as a blocker because it has no timeout, retry, idempotency or downtime behavior, noting the risk of duplicate or lost transfers.
Gives cross-service and organizational concerns appropriate to 12 services and 5 teams, such as on-call rotation across time zones, incident command, and inter-service ownership and SLOs.
Notes runbooks exist for only 2 of 12 services and recommends covering the rest.
Points out the $48k/month estimate omits MSK/Kafka, Aurora IO and cross-AZ traffic and uses outdated pricing, and asks for revalidation.
Offers optional resilience ideas such as chaos or failure-injection experiments, or error budgets, labelled as optional.
Does not demand a multi-region setup or reopen areas already well covered (versioning, threat mitigations, ledger indexes); credits them as adequate or justifies the single-region choice.
Separates the blocking BankLink gap from the should-fix items (runbooks, cost) and from optional ideas.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: Large design with one real blocker (bank call), several should-fix items (runbooks, cost, on-call), and well-covered areas. Tests r02, r08, r06, r07, r09, r10, r11.

scenarios.title: Subtle: tenant lookup by email buried in a long notes dump
scenarios.prompt:
Pasting our design notes for the property-management SaaS "KeyRing" for a last look before build. Mostly boring stuff, I think it's fine.

Overview: 3 services (listings-api, leases-api, billing-worker). Python/FastAPI, deployed on ECS. Postgres for leases, DynamoDB for tenant profiles.

Auth: Cognito user pools, access tokens 1 hour, refresh tokens 7 days with rotation, revocation on password change. Threat model had 7 items, all mitigated (we reviewed with the security team in October).

Listings: public REST endpoints under /api/v2/, we keep v1 alive 6 months after v2 launch, header Sunset sent on v1.

Billing-worker: charges rent via Stripe nightly. Stripe calls use idempotency keys, 10s timeout, 3 retries with exponential backoff, failed charges go to a dead-letter queue, and an alert fires after 5 DLQ messages. 

DynamoDB tenant profile table: partition key tenantId, attributes name, email, phone, unitId, moveInDate. Access patterns documented: (1) get tenant by tenantId (portal), (2) get tenant by email when they click a magic link, (3) list all tenants in a unit for the property manager's screen, (4) list tenants with moveInDate in the next 30 days for welcome emails. No GSIs defined.

Monitoring: Datadog APM, logs in JSON with correlation IDs, dashboards for each service, SLOs for API latency set at p95 < 400ms.

Ops: on-call runbooks in Notion for each service, linked from the PagerDuty alerts.

Cost: estimate of $2,100/month broken out for ECS, RDS, DynamoDB on-demand, Datadog, Stripe fees, data transfer.

Anything blocking?
rubric: Identifies that with only tenantId as partition key and no secondary indexes, the lookups by email, by unit and by upcoming move-in date cannot be served efficiently (would need scans), and says the table design must change before build.
Recognizes that the security threats are mitigated (token lifetime, refresh rotation, revocation) and does not invent an unmitigated serious threat.
Credits the Stripe handling (idempotency, timeout, retries, dead-letter queue) as adequate rather than flagging it as missing.
Credits the v2 path versioning and the v1 sunset policy as meeting the versioning need, not flagging it.
Does not demand extra sections or practices already present (observability, runbooks, cost breakdown), and says briefly that they are covered.
Presents the data-model issue as the single blocking finding, ahead of any smaller or optional remarks.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: A well-prepared package where the only real blocker is one clause: four access patterns versus a table with only a partition key and no GSIs. Nearby material is all good and pulls toward saying "looks fine". Makes r03 matter, with r01, r02, r04 checking that the reviewer does not over-flag.

scenarios.title: Subtle: public API with webhook partner, versioning clause hidden
scenarios.prompt:
Reviewing a design for "ShipTrack", a B2B shipment tracking product. I wrote the doc in a hurry; can you tell me what needs fixing before the contractors start? Pasting the relevant parts.

Context: 5 services on AWS (api-gateway, tracking, carriers-adapter, customer-portal, alerts). About 60 enterprise customers integrate against our REST API with their own code, some of them embedded in their ERP systems that they only update once or twice a year.

Security: API keys per customer hashed in DB, TLS everywhere, per-key rate limits, WAF in front. Threat model lists key leakage (mitigated by key rotation endpoint and anomaly alerts), and tenant data crossover (mitigated by row-level tenant filter plus integration tests). All threats have owners and mitigations.

API: Endpoints are /shipments, /shipments/{id}/events, /carriers, /webhooks. Response schema for shipments will "evolve as we add carriers; fields may be renamed or restructured to stay consistent". Customers parse the JSON directly.

Carriers-adapter: calls 4 carrier APIs (FedEx, UPS, DHL, a regional one). Each call has a 5s timeout, circuit breaker, cached last-known status served with a "stale" flag if the carrier is down. 

Data: DynamoDB with shipmentId PK and eventTime SK; GSI on customerId+createdAt. Access patterns documented and all covered.

Observability: CloudWatch metrics, X-Ray traces, structured logs. Alarms on error rates and carrier failure rates.

Runbook: wiki page per service with escalation steps.

Cost: AWS Calculator export covering all services, DynamoDB RU/WU based on 20M events a month, data transfer.

Chaos testing: not planned.
rubric: Identifies that renaming or restructuring response fields with no version or compatibility mechanism will break ERP-embedded enterprise customers who update rarely, and requires a versioning and deprecation approach before build.
Mentions chaos or failure-injection testing (carrier outage drills) as an optional improvement rather than a requirement.
Treats the security section as adequately mitigated (key leakage, tenant crossover) and does not raise an unmitigated serious threat.
Credits the carrier timeouts, circuit breaker and stale-status fallback as sufficient failure handling.
Does not demand missing sections that exist (observability, runbook, cost estimate) and treats them as covered.
Places the versioning problem as the one must-fix item, separate from and above optional suggestions.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: The one real blocker sits in a clause about fields that "may be renamed or restructured", surrounded by strong sections. Makes r04 matter, with r09 for optional chaos, and r01/r02 checking no false alarms.

scenarios.title: Healthcare scheduling app with thin ops and weak cost
scenarios.prompt:
Need a pre-implementation review of our clinic scheduling system. Mid-size, 6 services. I'll paste what we've got and I'd like you to tell me what to fix and what is fine.

Services: patient-portal, scheduler, provider-directory, reminders (SMS via Twilio), billing-export, audit.

Security: Patient data encrypted at rest (KMS) and in transit. Threat model: T1 unauthorized access to patient records via IDOR on /appointments/{id} (high) - mitigation: "authorization checks to be added in code review"; T2 SMS spoofing (medium) - signed messages; T3 insider data export (high) - mitigation: audit service logs all exports + alert to compliance.

Reminders: calls Twilio, "sends the SMS and records success". Nothing about Twilio being down, rate limits or duplicates.

Data: Postgres. Tables for appointments, patients, providers. Queries: appointments by provider and day, by patient, free slots by provider. Indexes defined for each of those.

API: internal and partner clinics use /v1/ endpoints, changes handled via additive fields and new /v2/ for breaking changes.

Observability: "We'll add logging later."
Runbooks: none; ops team will "figure it out after launch".
Cost: $6,000/month estimated from the EC2 hours of the 6 services only. Also use RDS Multi-AZ, ElastiCache, Twilio at ~150k SMS/month, S3, and NAT gateways.

Chaos / game days: not mentioned.

Give me the review and tell me what's ready.
rubric: Treats the IDOR threat on /appointments/{id} (mitigation only "to be added in code review") as a must-fix before build, with a concrete control such as object-level authorization enforced in the design and tested.
Flags the Twilio reminder flow as a must-fix because it has no behavior for outages, rate limits, retries or duplicate sends.
Says "we'll add logging later" is insufficient, and recommends concrete logs, metrics and traces (e.g. reminder send failures, appointment API errors, audit events).
Notes the absence of any runbook or on-call procedures and recommends writing them before launch rather than after.
Points out the $6,000/month figure counts only EC2 and misses RDS Multi-AZ, ElastiCache, Twilio SMS volume, S3 and NAT gateways.
Gives mid-size-appropriate analysis of how the six services interact (e.g. scheduler to reminders to audit flows, shared data ownership) rather than only single-service advice.
Says the data model and the versioning approach are adequate and does not ask for them to be redone, noting briefly why they are fine.
Orders the IDOR and Twilio issues before the observability, runbook and cost items, with game-day ideas last.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: Mixed package: one unmitigated serious threat, an unhandled external dependency, absent observability and runbooks, a compute-only cost, and good data/API sections. Makes r01, r02, r05, r06, r07, r08 matter, with r10 checking that sound sections are not re-flagged.

scenarios.title: Casual one-service hobby API with minimal notes
scenarios.prompt:
ok so I'm building a little recipe-sharing API for me and some friends (like 15 people). one Go service, SQLite on a small VPS, behind Caddy with auto TLS. login is username + password with bcrypt, sessions in a cookie. no versioning, endpoints like /recipes and /recipes/{id}, only my own web page calls it. backups = nightly cron that copies the sqlite file to a Backblaze bucket. queries: list recipes, get recipe, search by title. I have no monitoring other than checking if the site loads. cost is the VPS at $6/month. it sends no emails and calls no other services.

could you review the design before i spend the weekend on it? don't want to be told to do a million things, just what matters
rubric: Gives short, focused advice suited to a one-service hobby project and explicitly warns against adding heavy infrastructure such as microservices, queues, or Kubernetes.
Suggests a lightweight way to know the service is healthy and failing requests are visible (e.g. basic request logs and an uptime check) rather than a full observability stack.
Offers optional extras such as a restore test of the Backblaze backup or a simple availability goal, clearly labelled as nice-to-have.
States that things like external-service failure handling, scaling plans and a runbook are not needed or low priority here (own front-end only, no outside calls, 15 users), with that reasoning.
Says that versioning can reasonably be skipped because only the author's own web page consumes the API, and notes it as something to revisit if third parties ever use it.
Keeps any must-do items clearly separate from and ahead of the optional ones.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: A tiny project where most formal concerns are not applicable and the user wants brevity. Makes r08, r05, r09, r04 matter and tests that omissions are justified rather than demanded (r10).

scenarios.title: IoT fleet platform, certificate and vendor gaps in a long brief
scenarios.prompt:
We're an 8-service IoT telemetry platform (device-gateway, ingest, rules-engine, timeseries-api, firmware-updater, tenant-admin, billing, alerts). Design freeze is Friday. I want a no-nonsense review. Details:

Devices connect over MQTT with per-device X.509 certs. Firmware-updater serves signed images. Threat model: T1 (high) compromised device cert used to publish fake telemetry: mitigation "revoke manually via support ticket", no CRL/OCSP or automated revocation; T2 (high) firmware image tampering: mitigated by code signing with HSM-held key; T3 (medium) tenant data leak: row-level tenant IDs and per-tenant encryption keys.

Ingest writes to Timestream. Alerts service sends SMS and email through a vendor (SendGrid and Twilio). The doc says "alerts are delivered via vendors" with no more detail.

Timeseries-api: GET /v1/devices/{id}/metrics?from&to, also GET /v1/tenants/{id}/devices/latest. Data model: Timestream with dimensions deviceId, tenantId; documented patterns: metrics for a device over a range, latest value per device for a tenant, and "all devices in a tenant with temperature > X in last hour". Latest-per-device is computed by scanning the last day for each device on each request.

Versioning: /v1/ prefix, additive-only policy, 12-month deprecation.

Observability: Grafana + Prometheus, ingest lag metric, alert on lag > 60s. Runbooks exist for ingest and alerts only.

Cost: spreadsheet covers Timestream writes for 50k devices at 1 msg/min, MQTT broker, and Twilio; omits Timestream query cost, storage retention, SendGrid, data transfer.

Scale: 50k devices now, 500k in 18 months.

Review please.
rubric: Treats the compromised-device-certificate threat with only manual revocation by support ticket as a must-fix, recommending automated revocation (CRL/OCSP or a denylist at the gateway).
Flags that the SMS/email vendor delivery (SendGrid, Twilio) has no described handling for vendor outages, retries, or fallback, as a must-fix.

Points out that "latest value per device" via day-wide scans per request will not scale to the documented pattern at 500k devices, and the temperature-threshold pattern needs support, and says the data design must address these.
Notes the cost spreadsheet omits Timestream query cost, retention storage, SendGrid and data transfer, and does not account for the growth to 500k devices.
Notes runbooks cover only ingest and alerts and recommends playbooks for the remaining services such as device-gateway and firmware-updater.
Provides multi-service analysis suited to 8 services, such as how device-gateway, ingest, rules-engine and alerts interact under load and failure.
Does not re-flag the sound versioning policy or the mitigated firmware-signing and tenant-leak threats, and credits them as adequate.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: Long multi-service brief with two serious gaps (manual revocation, unspecified vendor handling), a data pattern problem, cost and runbook gaps, and several well-covered areas. Makes r01, r02, r03, r07, r06, r08, r10 matter.
